parent.name: Search & ranking
parent.one_liner: Filters out what cannot work, then scores and ranks the rest.
parent.explain: I take the renter's filters and every listing, and first drop the ones that cannot work, such as a rent over budget. Each survivor gets a fit score from 0 to 100, built from budget, commute distance and extras, with a plain reason per part. I sort by score, highest first, break ties with the lower rent, and return up to the limit, which defaults to 5. If fewer places fit than the limit, I also show listings that fail exactly one filter, so the renter knows what to loosen. Every search records an impression, a note that a listing was shown, for each match I return.
parent.why: Hard filters keep impossible places away from the renter, and the score puts the best fit first. Plain reasons let the AI explain why a place fits instead of guessing. Near misses stop a strict search from ending in an empty answer.

children.name: Hard filters
children.one_liner: Says in words which must-haves a listing fails.
children.explain: I check each listing against six filters: rent, bedrooms, pets, move-in date, must-have amenities and chosen neighborhoods. Every failed filter becomes a short sentence, such as a dollar amount over budget, or the list of missing amenities. For pets I use a small table, PET_OK, that says which listing policies suit a renter with no pet, a cat or a dog. An empty list means the listing passes, and I only score listings that come back empty.
children.why: Filters that fail in words let me show near misses and tell the renter exactly why a place was dropped. A silent yes or no would hide the one thing worth loosening. A listing that breaks a hard rule must never be scored as a good fit.

children.name: Fit score
children.one_liner: Averages budget, commute and extras into a 0-100 score.
children.explain: I score a listing with up to three parts, each between 0 and 1: budget fit, commute, and share of nice-to-have extras. Budget and commute each weigh 0.4 and extras weigh 0.2; I average only over the parts the renter actually asked about. The budget part reaches full marks when the rent is 25% under the maximum, and each part writes its own plain reason. I multiply the average by 100 and round it; with no parts at all I return 50 and 'matches your filters'.
children.why: Weights let a close, affordable place beat one that only has a long amenity list. Averaging only the parts that apply keeps a renter who skipped commute from being punished. The plain reasons are what lets the AI say why a place fits.

children.name: Commute distance
children.one_liner: Straight-line kilometres to a landmark, turned into a score.
children.explain: I measure the straight-line distance between a listing and a named landmark with the haversine formula, which treats Earth as a sphere. I use an Earth radius of 6371 km and real landmark coordinates that were looked up in Apple Maps. The commute score is 1 minus the distance divided by 5 km, so full marks at 0 km and zero from 5 km on. For the reason I also give walking minutes at 80 metres a minute, and I label it a straight line, not a route.
children.why: A straight line needs no routing service, so the demo works offline and gives the same answer every time. Labelling it a straight line keeps me from promising a walking route I did not compute. Real coordinates keep the distances believable.

children.name: Near misses
children.one_liner: Shows listings that fail just one filter, with the reason.
children.explain: When fewer listings fit than the limit, I look at the listings that were dropped and keep those that fail exactly one filter. I sort them by fewest failures, then lower rent, and fill only the empty spots up to the limit. Each near miss comes with why_not, the failed filter in words, so the renter learns which single filter to loosen. Separately, search writes an impression row, a record that a listing was shown, for every match I return.
children.why: A strict search that returns nothing leaves the renter stuck. One named filter to loosen is an easy next step. Logging impressions records what was shown, without storing anything about the renter.
